utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-10-A, the Prosecutor versus Goran Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, the appearances are as before. The proceedings continue. We now have before us the cross-appeal. Ready, Mr. Clegg?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Ready. Can I indicate to the Chamber that Mr. Babic will be relieving me of some of the burden this morning, and we are dividing our submissions into two halves so far as sentence is concerned. The Court will have observed that the appellant's brief concentrated on the conduct of the trial Judge both during the course of the trial on genocide, where verdicts were returned in favour of the accused, and also during the protracted sentence hearings, when a large number of witnesses were called to the effect that, prior to the conflict in the former Yugoslavia, the appellant had exhibited no signs of racial prejudice against Muslims and had ongoing good relations with a number of people from that faith. We, of course, rely upon the evidence that was called during the sentencing hearing to establish those two facts, but I do not press today the criticism of the trial Judge during the hearing on genocide because, of course, that was a trial in which none of the offences for which he was being sentenced were being examined by the Trial Chamber. The position so far as the facts that gave rise to the pleas of guilty before the Trial Chamber is that, following lengthy consideration by both parties, an agreed statement of facts was arrived at. It was incorporated into an amended indictment and the appellant pleaded guilty on that basis. I am confident that this Appeals Chamber will deal with his sentence on the basis of those agreed facts and on no other basis. Obviously, he cannot be prejudiced as a result of the fact that he stood trial for another offence of which he was acquitted. The basis on which he pleaded guilty, having been agreed between the parties, must remain the basis upon which he was sentenced. It is our submission that the sentence passed of 40 years' imprisonment is excessive. The primary ground of appeal is that the Trial Chamber did not give sufficient attention to the need to develop a range of sentences based upon the relative position of the accused. The judgement of the Trial Chamber was given in December of 1999. It did therefore not have the benefit of the opinion of the Appeal Chamber delivered the following month in January 2000 in the appeal of Dusko Tadic. The Appeal Chamber in the Tadic case reduced the sentence of Tadic to one of 20 years, and the basis upon which the sentence was so reduced was primarily upon the second ground advanced by the appellant, namely, an error committed by the Trial Chamber with respect to the need to develop a range of sentences based upon the relative position of an accused. And we would commend to the Court pages 23, 24, and 25 of the Tadic Sentencing Judgement. At paragraph 55, the Appeal Chamber came to the considered opinion that the sentence passed failed to adequately consider the need for sentences to reflect the significance of the role of the appellant in the broader context of the conflict in the former Yugoslavia. It is our submission that had the Trial Chamber in the instant case had the benefit of considering the Appeal Chamber's views in the Tadic case, that it would not and could not have passed the sentence that it did of 40 years' imprisonment. A study of the facts, in our submission, reveals nothing to choose between the two cases. Each involved the commission of a number of murders against victims of a different ethnic background or religion. The number and type of murders in both cases was broadly similar. They included in each case the brutal execution of helpless victims, and the Court will remember, some of the Court I know will remember, the two convictions of Tadic for killing the two policemen by slitting their throats in the village that he and others had taken during the course of that conflict. His, Tadic's, guilt embraced not only ethnic cleansing of more than one village, but also, of course, his cruel mistreatment of victims in a detention camp, cruelty that would justify all of the well-deserved adjectives applied to the actions of Jelisic in the instant case. If anything, the cruelty in the Tadic case was worse, embracing a degree of sado-sexual mistreatment, including the biting off of a man's testicle. We would submit that on any broad comparison of the facts of the two cases that there can be little to choose between them. Neither had a command position. They were both, in every sense, men of low position in the broader context of the conflict. Neither were commanders or architects of the strategy of ethnic cleansing. Of course, each was a willing executioner. One of the facts that emerges from any study of war crimes, both contemporary and historical, is that it is within the capacity of all to act as camp guards and executioners, and one has only to reflect on the ill-treatment that occurred in the Second World War of camp detainees throughout Europe to see powerful evidence of that. The fact that both these men were willing, if not enthusiastic, in their ill-treatment of detainees, sadly, in the history of war crimes, is not either remarkable or unusual. The fact remains that neither were in a command position; neither were the architects of the strategy of ethnic cleansing. Both were, in truth, foot soldiers, not in positions of command. Of course, positions of power over those that were detained. Every camp guard is in a position of power, but that is different from a position of command. The sentences are a stark contrast. Tadic, a man of mature years who pleaded not guilty and contested the case vehemently throughout received an ultimate total sentence of 20 years. Jelisic, a young man in his early 20s who pleaded guilty at the very outset, received twice that figure of 40 years. Whilst I am not praying in aid the psychological problems of Jelisic in a way that would significantly mitigate his conduct, it is a fact that he did suffer a severe personality disorder. No such excuse existed in the Tadic case for his conduct. The aggravating features identified in the Jelisic case by the Trial Chamber all existed in the Tadic case. There is nothing, we submit, in truth to distinguish one case from the other. Now, it is our respectful submission that it be of vital importance to the ongoing reputation of this Court that consistent sentences are passed for broadly similar conduct. Nothing will bring a criminal justice system more into disrepute than the appearance that its decisions are capricious, inconsistent, or driven by personal dislike of an individual. Of course, in a sense, anyone who had to listen to the evidence on the genocide trial may unconsciously have been influenced against the defendant Jelisic when it came to sentence him for what he, in fact, admitted, which, so far as the indictment is concerned, involved some 12 murders and other offences of ill-treatment. It is not just the Tadic Judgement upon which we rely to demonstrate what we submit is an inconsistent approach by the Trial Chamber in this court. The written brief submitted on the appellant's behalf analyses the case of Erdemovic, which Mr. Babic had the advantage of appearing in. I don't intend to repeat all that he has written about that case in the brief. Repetition does not advance any point submitted to this Trial Chamber, but we commend what he has said. Other decisions both here and in Rwanda also highlight the contrast identified by an analysis of the Tadic Judgement. In the Rwanda case of Serushago and the Prosecutor, judgement again being given after the judgement in this case and therefore not a case that the Trial Chamber would have been able to consider when deciding where, in the broad range of sentences, it was right to position an appellant here, a sentence of 15 years' imprisonment for genocide was upheld by the Appeal Chamber. That embraced crimes against humanity, murder, extermination, and torture, killing vastly more people than ever lost their life in this part of the former Yugoslavia, let alone justifying any comparison with the numbers in fact killed by Jelisic. In the Serushago case, over 300 victims were killed in just one incident. He, Serushago, of course, was in a position of command, quite different from that of Jelisic. In giving judgement, this Appeal Chamber, in considering the sentence of 15 years' imprisonment for genocide in that case, said at paragraph 33 of the judgement that it was "within the discretionary framework" of the Trial Chamber to pass such a sentence. What we ask rhetorically, that if that be right, as we submit it was, that 15 years was within the discretionary framework for the crime of genocide when hundreds of thousands have been killed as a consequence of the actions of somebody who held a position of command, then how, we say rhetorically, can a sentence of 40 years in this case be justified? There is, in truth, no fair comparison to be made. In the Kayishema and Ruzindena Judgement, another Rwandan case, the Court had to consider what was described as planned, instigated, ordered, widespread killings on a vast scale. Both men were guilty of genocide. The Court distinguished between them on the basis of their rank. Ruzindena, at paragraph 543 of the judgement, was described in the following manner: "as someone who played a leadership role in the systematic pattern of the extermination of the Tutsis who had sought refuge in the area of Besaro. He led attacks on them where thousands were killed." And I quote from the judgement, at paragraph 542, the following words: "They were killed regardless of gender or age. Men and women, old and young, were killed without mercy. Children were massacred before their parents' eyes; women raped in front of their families. No Tutsi was spared, neither the weak nor the pregnant." For planning and putting into operation that genocide, the sentence of 25 years' imprisonment was passed on Ruzindena. Moving to the former Yugoslavia, the Celebici case is also instructive. Mucic was the commander of the camp; he was sentenced to seven years for murder and cruel treatment. Delic, 20 years, murder, torture, wilfully causing great suffering and serious bodily harm. Landzo, a young man, I think but 23, 15 years for murder, torture, and suffering. A quote from the Court's description of him is perhaps relevant when looking at the adjectives properly described to the conduct of Jelisic in this case. Of Landzo, who received a sentence of 15 years, the Tribunal said: "The nature of his crimes is suggestive of significant imagination and a perverse pleasure in the infliction of pain and suffering." It's not attractive to try to choose adjectives to describe the type of conduct that this Court and the Tribunal in Rwanda has to sit in judgement over. There is, in truth, no adjectives available in any language of the world to properly describe and condemn the conduct these Courts need to deal with. In fact, the only guide to sentence in such a case must be, we submit, the guidance of other cases and the development of a tariff that ensures that there is a just disposition of cases, one weighed against the other. This Court I know is conscious of the fact that it is not just, of course, the punishment of the crimes that is relevant, but the role that the Court needs to play in the ultimate rehabilitation of the area of Europe where this conflict has been fought over. Moving on to the Blaskic case. Here the Court had to deal with a commander, a decision-maker near the very top of the chain of command, a General under whose command vast numbers of people were killed. It was accepted by the Tribunal that he ordered the widespread extermination of Muslims, including the massacre at Ahmici, but not confined to it. The Trial Chamber described that massacre in these words: "A carefully prepared attack, many Muslim children, women, and adults were systematically murdered, sometimes burnt alive in their home, houses plundered and set alight, mosques and religious buildings destroyed." In the Kupreskic case there were six defendants. It also, of course, involved the massacre at Ahmici on the 16th of April 1993 when 116 people were killed in the attack that I have just described. The Court in that case said that the village of Ahmici had gone down in history as comprising one of the most vicious illustrations of man's inhumanity to man, and compared the name of the village in the same sentence as that of Dachau and My Lai. The sentences passed for those actively involved in that attack, Zoran Kupreskic, eight years; his brother, Vlatko, six years; Papic, 15; Santic, who was the commander of the company, 25 years. It's against that background that we submit that the sentence here of 40 years is significantly out of step with other sentences passed by both this Tribunal and that dealing with crimes in Rwanda. In applying the passage that I've already alluded to in the Tadic Judgement, we would submit that it falls significantly outside the range of sentences that has, since judgement was passed, developed more clearly, perhaps, than it had before. When compared with the Tadic case, we say that there are very broad similarities, and we bluntly and boldly submit to the Appeal Chamber that if the proper sentence in Tadic was one of 20 years, then we submit that there could be no justification on a comparable basis for passing any longer sentence in the instant appeal. May I say a few words about rank. Jelisic did not hold any rank. He was not a commander. His plea was accepted on that basis, and in our submission, he must stand to be dealt with in accordance with that agreed plea. When he was first arraigned before the Court, his first indictment at page 10 alleged that during most of May of 1992, he acted as commander of Luka camp. That was a matter that was the subject of dispute by him, and the words were deleted by agreement from the agreed statement of facts that formed the basis of his plea. Once those pleas were accepted, the Court, in our submission, cannot go behind that agreed position. Against that background, paragraph 95 of the judgement is unfortunately phrased. It begins with the following words: "It has also not been established beyond all reasonable doubt whether the accused killed at Luka camp under orders. Goran Jelisic allegedly presented himself to the detainees as the Luka camp commander"; and concludes, "The Trial Chamber does not doubt that the accused exercised a de facto authority over the staff and detainees at the camp." The position, in truth, is that the allegation that he was in command had been expressly deleted from the agreed factual basis upon which he tendered his pleas. What this paragraph, I submit, probably identifies and is alluding to is that everybody who is at a camp such as that in a guard role has a position of power over the detainees that Jelisic, as others in the past have, abused. And of course, somebody with a position of power will be viewed as having the power to command by those over whom he exercises that power. It is a perfectly natural, human reaction. It does not mean in fact, of course, that he is the commander of the camp in the sense that he is ordering and directing the ill-treatment and murder of detainees over and above that which he is personally responsible for. And indeed, of course, the charges to which he pled only relate to his own physical acts of murder and ill-treatment, and he did Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. not fall to be sentenced upon the basis of what others may have done in the same institution on some other occasion. In our submission, the distinction between someone who is in a position of command has been recognised consistently by this Court when the Court has moved to consider sentence. This man must be dealt with on the basis that he had no rank. May I move now to consider his plea of guilty. In our submission, that ought to attract a discount in sentence. It is a plea of guilty that he tendered against the advice of his then lawyers who advised him, wrongly I would submit, that he had a proper defence to the allegation of crimes against humanity. But in the face of the advice of his own lawyers, he tendered the pleas that he did. A plea of guilty in most jurisdictions of the world will attract a discount in sentence. The reasons are, in part, pragmatic because most criminal justice systems can only survive where a significant number of people do admit their guilt; otherwise, the systems of justice throughout the world would collapse under the weight of work. The whole philosophy behind plea bargaining in the United States of America is primarily pragmatic. In our submission, this Chamber as well ought to send out a signal to those who are in detention and those who await arrest that pleas of guilty will attract a discount in sentence, particularly perhaps when tendered against the advice of trial counsel. A plea of guilty, of course, is separate from remorse. A plea of guilty may be tendered for pragmatic reasons, just as a discount for sentence may be given for pragmatic reasons. It does not follow that a man who pleads guilty has remorse; of course I accept that. It is always difficult in a common law jurisdiction for a defendant to convince a court that he does have remorse. Here in this trial, the defendant was, I almost said, denied the opportunity of giving evidence in the trial. He never had an opportunity because the trial ended at the end of the Prosecution case. So the Court never had, in fact, the opportunity to judge him themselves through sworn testimony. In many ways, it's difficult to believe that somebody who acted in the way that he did could have remorse. But we do submit that the Trial Chamber misdirected itself as to the burden that the accused had to discharge in order to convince them that he had remorse. It's at paragraph 127 of the judgement where, we submit, the Trial Chamber fell into error. The first sentence reads: "The Trial Chamber is not convinced that the remorse which Goran Jelisic allegedly expressed to the expert psychiatrist was sincere." I venture to suggest that in the vast majority of cases, both internationally and nationally, a court can very rarely be convinced of someone's remorse. Everyone is going to express remorse when they admit crime, or, at any rate, almost everyone. It's not, we submit, for a defendant to have to satisfy the Court that his remorse is genuine. We would respectfully submit that in circumstances such as those that existed here, a Trial Chamber ought to accept expressions of remorse that were accepted as sincere by an expert psychiatrist unless it was convinced that the expressions of remorse were false. We would, with respect, as it were, reverse the evidential approach of the Trial Chamber at paragraph 127. The position before the Trial Chamber was that remorse was expressed in the traditional way it is done in common law jurisdictions; namely, through the mouth of his advocate, through his pleas of guilty to the indictment, through his admission, despite the absence of evidence, of three murders that he had not been indicted for, through the extensive interviews that he willingly gave to the investigators, and the evidence of the witnesses, in particular DQ, DF, and DA, to which reference is made in the written brief. Finally, for the matters that I intend to cover before I hand the floor to Mr. Babic, there is the question of his youth. He was but 23 years old at the time he committed these crimes. No defence, of course. But this Tribunal has consistently accepted youth as mitigation. In the Landzo case it did, when he was 19; in Erdemovic, when he was 23; and in Furundzija, when he was also 23. I quote from the footnote 1696 in the Blaskic Judgement, at page 255, the following words: "The ICTY considers accused aged between 19 and 23 at the time of the facts as being young." And youth, in the Blaskic Judgement at that page, was expressly identified as a mitigating circumstance. Indeed, the Trial Chamber itself clearly hoped that with appropriate medical and psychiatric assistance during the prison sentence Jelisic will inevitably serve, he will be able to be rehabilitated, as they recommended that he undergo psychological and psychiatric treatment in whichever host country accepts him as a prisoner. Those are the submissions that I advance on behalf of the appellant. I'd now ask for Mr. Babic to address the Court on the remaining grounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Clegg, may I have a clarification from you. During your arguments, you mentioned that the Trial Chamber may have been influenced by the evidence heard during the trial on genocide in deciding the sentence to be imposed for the crimes to which Mr. Jelisic pleaded guilty. Can you clarify one matter to me, whether it is your position that the Trial Chamber should not have taken into account such evidence, and that if it did so, it may have incurred an error either of law or of fact, or both possibly, that the Appeal Chamber should take into account and consider under Article 25 of the Statute. I would like to know which is your position in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Certainly. The crime of genocide and the trial of genocide embraced facts far greater than he had pleaded guilty to. Insofar as the evidence before the Trial Chamber dealt with the counts on the indictment to which he had pleaded, then I would accept that the Trial Chamber could consider that evidence, but I would submit it should do so cautiously because it was not being cross-examined as to mitigation but being cross-examined solely as to its applicability to the allegation of genocide. But I concede the Trial Chamber could look at the evidence, as it were, on the individual counts. But the evidence before the Trial Chamber on the genocide trial went far wider than the agreed facts, and indeed, went behind the agreed facts by asserting a factual position that had expressly been abandoned at the time of plea. The Trial Chamber ought not to be influenced by any of that evidence but should be confined to the agreed facts. Just an illustration is the fact that there was an allegation that he was the camp commander. Now, although that was abandoned by the Prosecution in the agreed statement of facts and his plea was accepted on that basis, when giving evidence, witnesses, of course, spoke of him as the camp commander. Now, the Trial Chamber would not be entitled to sentence him on the basis of that evidence, that he held a position of command, because that would go behind the agreed factual basis upon which his plea had been tendered. But insofar as they might describe an act of cruelty to which he had pleaded, then in considering how he committed the actual offence to which he pleaded, then they could have recourse to that. So I don't know if that answers the question that I've been posed. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Clegg, following, following up on that, can you give us a little more information on whether or not the position you have just espoused you think is a majority, a plurality, a universal norm? I'm sure you're familiar with the departure from that in the case of the United States where the Supreme Court has actually said that evidence and the fact of an acquittal in one count, or even in one crime, may be taken into consideration in the sentencing for other crimes. A controversial, admittedly, a holding, but nonetheless a holding. So I wonder if your answer to Judge Pocar could be elaborated on, whether or not you think your position is one that's more universal, say, than the one I have just set out.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Well, I would respectfully submit that the one I have just expounded is more universal. It would be the only approach that would be consistent with the European convention on human rights because there could be, we would submit, no fair trial under Article 5 or 6 of the convention if the Court were to consider, as it were, to go behind, an agreed statement of facts upon which a plea was tendered. That would certainly be my submission under European law. I anticipate this in most common law jurisdictions, the position that I have just expounded is the basis upon which the Court would approach sentence. It would be honest of me to confess that I didn't have the judgement of the American Supreme Court at the forefront of my mind this morning when I was addressing the Chamber. It does seem on the face of it a judgement would have difficulty in surviving in the European Court. I don't know if I can assist any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Clegg, I think all jurists would respond positively to your main submission that a Court should not suffer itself to appear to be acting capriciously, but also I take it you accept, basically, sentence depends on the Court's view of the facts of each case. I understand you to be saying, yes, the Court has a discretion in sentencing, but that that discretion has to be exercised with reference to discernible principles of law. And your analysis of the various cases leads you to extract from them a principle which says, roughly, that sentences should lie within a certain range. Maybe an undefining range, but a discernible one. So that wide as the discretion is, if the discretion is not exercised with reference to that principle of law which you submit can be extracted from the various cases, then the sentence is wrong, decision is wrong. But tell me this: Narrow as that range may be, does it exclude, for example, the competence of the Court to impose a life sentence, and has the Court in fact imposed a life sentence, I think, in the case of the Rwanda Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: It in no way precludes a life sentence being passed in an appropriate case. The life sentence in genocide was, I think, passed for an offence -- the life sentence to which you allude was for an offence of genocide, and the defendant was, I think, either the prime minister or certainly a very senior government official who was orchestrating the extermination of tens or thousands of Tutsis. I would not suggest for one moment that a life sentence in such circumstances was outside any range of sentencing. Indeed, where the Rules of the Tribunal expressly make provision for the sentence -- for a life sentence, it follows that in an appropriate case a life sentence will be appropriate. But it must, of course, be reserved for the most heinous of crimes, and we would submit that in practice, it will probably be reserved for those who commanded and orchestrated genocide. I hope that deals --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You have dealt with the part. I understand you to be saying that for cases of this type, there is a certain range of sentences --

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: -- and that the sentence imposed was outside of the applicable range. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: That is our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: And indeed, 40 years is getting very near a life sentence when one works out what the average life expectancy of a man his age is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Any more questions. Thank you, then, Mr. Clegg. Mr. Babic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am, in a sense, continuing the Defence, as the Prosecutor yesterday said that he was continuing the Prosecution. I have no intention of using that position in the way that Mr. Nice did, by making certain statements which are not grounded in the brief or to encourage certain thinking by the Trial Chamber at the expense of the accused. What I have in mind is the reference to 2.000 dead as being undisputed even though it is clearly in dispute, and also reference by Mr. Nice to certain evidence that has not been proven. I would appeal to Your Honours to bear that in mind when reviewing this case. Mr. Nice also referred to a list given to the guards and the prison administration, saying that all those people were killed, which is also not correct, because in the proceedings, they were proven to be alive and certain documents confirmed that. He also referred to testimony by IBNR, the statement of witness Ralston -- the statement by witness Ralston, and let me just say that he stated that throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina, a total of 3.000 civilians had been killed in Bosnia - 3.000 civilians. So this cannot be the kind of evidence that Mr. Nice described it as being. I would just like to highlight a few points which I consider to be important within the time allotted to us, and perhaps then in the rebuttal we will have a chance to say a few more words. I would suggest that a part of my argument be in open session, but I would appeal to Their Honours to allow us to go into private session for another part of my statement, which will come at the end. Mr. Clegg spoke about the plea of guilty which should be taken into account when sentencing. I should just like to add to what has already been said by Mr. Clegg, the following: The accused showed consciousness of his guilt before making a plea in the Trial Chamber, even before coming to the Tribunal. He had told Witnesses DO, DF, DA, and DQ clearly what he had done and shown remorse.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: A second point I wish to make --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, I am advised that the witness to whom you are now referring testified in closed session. Does that present you with a problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In view of the fact that I have not, in any way, identified them, I think this should not be a problem at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you for that remark. I take it, then, that you intend to proceed on the basis that there will be no identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no intention of identifying them, and I shall be very careful, Your Honours. Maybe I will be repeating something Mr. Clegg said, but the accused did admit, contrary to his Defence counsel's advice, three additional murders with which he was not charged or accused of, and I think this should be taken into account. Also, as Mr. Clegg pointed out, the result of admission was based on an agreed statement of facts, and it was on the basis of that agreed statement of facts that another indictment was issued, that the indictment was amended. That is why no new witnesses were called, no other evidence presented, and all the material expenses saved, all the things that are implied when a plea of guilty is entered. Mr. Clegg spoke about the sincerity of remorse, and I will refer again to the statements of the same witnesses to support that. I should also refer to the statements of the accused himself, because the Trial Chamber said that the accused did not manifest his remorse to the Trial Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Chamber, but let me refer to a statement of the appellant. During his repeated plea, when he admitted the offences, he stated before the Trial Chamber that he had made his plea -- that he had entered his plea of guilty voluntarily, unconditionally, and that, in that way, he wanted to clear his soul. That was stated in 1998. In response to a question by the President of this Appeals Chamber at the Status Conference on the 4th of April about how he felt in detention, the defendant replied, "Sorrow, remorse, and shame," thereby clearly showing how he was feeling about his crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: and also the finding of the psychiatrists regarding the appellant. May I also refer to a note I took when talking to Mr. McFadden on the 7th of September last year, the commander of the Detention Unit. The discussion referred to the condition of Mr. Jelisic. I asked him what his assessment was of his condition, and Mr. McFadden said the following and I took it down word by word: "Jelisic is a victim in many ways. He has a disturbed personality because he knows that he did bad things. And if there was a way for him to make up for it, I am sure that he would do it." I think this testifies to the remorse that the appellant expressed in his conversation with Mr. McFadden. Other Defence witnesses also said that Goran Jelisic committed his crimes -- I beg your pardon. I skipped a part. All this shows beyond any reasonable doubt that Goran Jelisic feels sincere remorse for the crimes he has committed, because he who has sincere remorse does not ask God or this Honourable Trial Chamber's pardon but for a sentence he deserves. And may I say once again that 40 years is a sentence that he deserves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Just for my information, what are you reading from? What text are you reading from?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are my handwritten notes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I thought you were reading a statement by someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had read what Mr. McFadden told me when I visited the Detention Unit. I would also like to point out that all the witnesses I have mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, Mr. Babic, that is not part of the record, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. It's not in the record. Can I explain? I asked Mr. McFadden whether he would send a report to Their Honours on Jelisic's behaviour in detention. Mr. McFadden answered that nobody had asked him to do that; however, as far as he was concerned, he would convey his own opinion, and that is what he did. That is what he told me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, the point is that the Appeals Chamber can only listen to the case on the basis of the record before it. Now, what my colleague on my left asked you was whether the material which you are now presenting forms any part of the record which we are to consider. It does not. Do I understand you?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McFadden did report to the Trial Chamber on the behaviour of Mr. Jelisic up to that time in detention. I went to see him a year later, whether he would report on his behaviour after that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: That may very well have been the case, but what my colleague on my left wanted to know was whether any of this forms part of the written documentation now before the Appeals Chamber. Can you point any pages in the record before us which would reflect the material which you are now putting before us?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
