utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I do remember the application that I made, and I'm quite sure we will keep to the time that has been allotted. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUARIGLIA
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I shall be very brief and honour our commitment to remain within the boundaries of our time limit. Your Honours, first I may have to bother you with something that you already know but that, nonetheless, we submit requires to be restated. It is, what is the scope of appellate review of sentences imposed by trial Chambers since it is the position of the Prosecution that the Defence may have misstated the exact scope of that review once the sentence has been imposed by a Trial Chamber. At the outset, the purpose of appellate proceedings, and this has been recently restated and clarified by the Celebici decision of this Appeals Chamber, the purpose of appellate proceedings is not for the Appeals Chamber to reconsider the evidence and factors submitted before the Trial Chamber. Second, the appellate process itself is not a forum to provide the parties with a supplementary chance to remedy their own failings or oversights during sentencing procedures within trial procedures. Third, your scope of examination is confined to determine whether a Trial Chamber, in imposing a sentence in a given case, committed an error of law by not taking into consideration factors established in the applicable provisions governing ICTY proceedings, that is, Article 24 of the Statute, Rule 101 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence ; or whether the Trial Chamber abused its discretion under those provisions. In both cases, that error, under the clear jurisprudence of this body stemming from the Tadic sentencing appeals, reaffirmed in the Furundzija Appeals Judgement and now again in the Celebici Appeals Judgement, must be a discernible one. Absent a showing by the appellant of a discernible error committed by the Trial Chamber in exercising its discretion in the imposition of an appropriate sentence, that sentence of the Trial Chamber remains undisturbed, and you shouldn't be asked to go beyond the limits of that very precise and very narrow scope of appellate review. The cornerstone of sentencing proceedings and imposition of sentence in this institution, as recognised by this Appellate Court, is that Trial Chambers exercise a considerable amount of discretion, although not unlimited, in determining the appropriate sentence; and that the, perhaps, main pillar for that intellectual process of determining what the appropriate sentence is, is the gravity of the crime attributed to the accused and of which the accused has been convicted. That takes me to one of the first submissions by my learned friend, this alleged need to establish a recognised tariff of sentences in the International Tribunal. I would respectfully submit that such a need simply does not exist. We add that in the recent Celebici Judgement, the Appeals Chamber declined to follow a similar, to some extent, invitation of the Prosecution to develop a list of basic principles for sentencing. The reasoning of the Appeals Chamber was that such a list would be of no value and that Trial Chambers must always honour their overriding obligation to individualise a penalty to fit the individual circumstances of the case and the gravity of the crime. I am quoting paragraph 717 of the Celebici Judgement. The Appeals Chamber noted in that decision, which appears to be in line with a prior finding of this Appeals Chamber in the Furundzija case, that it was premature to speak of a regime in relation to sentences in the International Tribunal. The Appeals Chamber in the Celebici decision, I repeat, considered that it may be that as the number of sentences imposed by Trial Chambers of this institution increase, there will be an emerging body of law which Trial Chambers will be obliged to consider for sentencing purposes but not bound to consider for the very same purposes. The rationale behind it: Trial Chambers must retain the sufficient margin of discretion, as granted by the Statute and the Rules, to impose the sentence that best reflects the gravity of the crime committed by an accused and his culpability or her culpability. That also means that a comparison between different cases and different sentences imposed in different cases is of limited or no value at all, and this has also been established by this Appeals Chamber in the recent Celebici decision; it is a clear finding, saying that often the differences between the cases are more significant than the similarities, and the mitigating and aggravating factors dictate different results. Comparing different cases of the International Tribunal is, then, an exercise of very, very limited value, and in the case at bar, the examples that have been provided by my learned friend are, we respectfully submit, misleading in a number of ways. A simple example, because I do not intend to spend more time on this, is the reliance on the Erdemovic case as a similar case, which simply ignores the enormous differences between the nature of both cases, the conduct of both accused, and the findings of both Trial Chambers. In the case of Erdemovic, there's a clear subjective difference with the case of the appellant in this proceedings. Erdemovic was characterised, was found to be, a reluctant executioner, someone who had been, to a large extent, coerced to engage in criminal activity; a perpetrator that was tormented by remorse, and that remorse being genuine; a perpetrator who had confessed his crimes before there was any prosecution against him. Now, the findings of Erdemovic and the sentence imposed on Erdemovic in the light of these very particular circumstances, we respectfully submit, cannot possibly be applied to the case of an accused whose behaviour has been found to be repugnant, bestial, and sadistic, the judgement of the Jelisic Trial Chamber, at paragraph 130; nor to someone whose cold-blooded commission of murders and mistreatment of people attest to a profound contempt for mankind and the right to life, same paragraph of the judgement; nor can they apply to a person who enthusiastically committed his crimes and took advantage of the opportunity afforded to him, by the feeling of power, to impose his own will on the defenceless victims and to decide who would live and who would die. We would respectfully submit it is untenable to sustain that someone who willingly and enthusiastically engaged in criminal activity of this nature should be compared with a reluctant executioner, tormented by remorse, as would be the case of Erdemovic. This shows again that cases before the International Tribunal should be treated individually, and that the discretion granted by the Statute and the rulings from Trial Chambers serves a purpose, and that purpose is to allow Chambers to individualise the correct sentence for each case. Same must be said about this allegation that under the law of this institution, the rank or the relative rank of an accused gives rise to some entitlement to obtain a lesser sentence; or put the other way around, that the higher you go in the chain of command, the more serious sentencing should be, the further down you go in the chain of command, the more lenient sentences should be. And we submit that the appellant's reliance on the Tadic sentencing appeals is misplaced. The decision of this Appellant Court in the Tadic sentencing appeals cannot and should not be read as one establishing an automatic right to mitigation in the case of low-level perpetrators. And here again, this particular issue has been clarified, conclusively clarified, we submit, in the recent Celebici Judgement of the Appeals Chamber whereby it can be read that: "The Tadic Sentencing Appeal Judgement ... did not purport to require that, in every case before it, an accused's level in the overall hierarchy in the conflict in the former Yugoslavia should be compared with those at the highest level, such that if the accused's place was such by comparison low, a low sentence should automatically be imposed. Establishing a gradation does not entail a low sentence for all those in a low level of the overall command structure. A sentence must always reflect the inherent level of gravity of a crime....In certain circumstances, the gravity of the crime may be so great that even following consideration of any mitigating factors, and despite the fact that the accused was not senior in the so-called overall command structure, a very severe penalty is nonetheless justified." I'm sorry to have to bother Your Honours with reading these findings, but this is a very recent decision and we submit it goes right to the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Could you kindly state the paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUARIGLIA
utterances.text: Yes, I was going to do that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: -- so that when we read the transcript, we will be able to identify exactly what is the passage you are referring to and find it easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUARIGLIA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's paragraph 847, and I was going to make that clear now. So, Your Honour, the position of the Prosecution I think is clear. The Trial Chamber in its judgement took into account all mitigating factors as established by the Statute and the pertinent Rules. What the appellant seems to be complaining of is that the Trial Chamber allegedly did not attach the sufficient weight to some of those factors. We would respectfully submit, Your Honour, that the weight to be attached to a particular mitigating factor is a matter that arises within the discretion of the Trial Chamber and should, absent a showing of an abuse of discretion, remain undisturbed. There is no doubt, and I don't think it has been submitted otherwise, that the Trial Chamber did consider all factors. Let's take the youth of the accused. The youth of the accused was an issue expressly dealt with by the Trial Chamber in its judgement at paragraph 124. It was extensively litigated during sentencing procedures. In closing argument, counsel for the appellant referred to the appellant as a "young man" at least seven times. This is not a forum, we repeat, where an appellant can come and attempt to relitigate issues that were discussed and were addressed before a Trial Chamber after the Trial Chamber has made its decision. Finally, Your Honours, two brief points: It wasn't very clear to the Prosecution what type of error the appellant was alleging as far as the consideration of the sentencing practice of courts of the former Yugoslavia is concerned. We have responded in writing extensively to the arguments raised at that point in time by the appellant in his appeal brief. We will only here repeat what is at this stage "jurisprudence constante" of this Appellate Court: Trial Chambers are not bound by the practice of the courts in the former Yugoslavia. This principle as stated by the Celebici decision of this Appeals Chamber at paragraphs 813 and 816 applies to crimes committed both before and after the Tribunal's establishment; and this issue was also, we repeat, fully litigated during sentencing proceedings before the Trial Chamber with counsel for the appellant providing the Trial Chamber with decisions from some courts in the former Yugoslavia which were considered by the Trial Chamber, and they were given the weight that the Trial Chamber considered appropriate. Your Honours, the overarching finding of the Trial Chamber in the case of the appellant was that considering all mitigating circumstances established in the Statute and the Rules and that had been advanced by the appellant during sentencing proceedings, and balancing those mitigating circumstances against those aggravating circumstances that had been established by the Prosecution during the same sentencing proceedings, the final conclusion was the aggravating circumstances far outweighed the mitigating circumstances, and that is the main premise on the basis of which that particular sentence was imposed on the appellant. And we submit there is no showing of a discernible error by the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. appellant; there is no showing of an abuse of discretion by the Trial Chamber; and we respectfully submit that absent such a showing, that discretion should remain undisturbed and that you should refrain from intervening when a showing of this nature has not been made. That concludes my submissions, Your Honours, and I will leave now, with your leave, the floor to Mr. Geoffrey Nice who will address some of the particular issues pertaining to this ground of appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I, too, hope to be brief. With absolutely no suggestion of complaint, we, of course, face today a slightly differently presented argument from that which was forecast in the larger pleading at an earlier stage submitted by the appellant. Our position is that we stand by all our arguments in our full response to that larger pleading but seek to amplify that response by our observations today in replying to what our two friends opposite have argued. Very briefly before I turn to the somewhat disconnected handful of points I have to deal with, Mr. Babic raised an issue that really relates to yesterday's hearing about things that I said, but it is important for me to point you to where this matter can properly be resolved. In our brief on the genocide issue, and he was harking back to that, at paragraph 4.62 I set out -- or rather, we set out in full the position of the evidence of 2.000 or 3.000 dead and so on, and I stand exactly by what I said yesterday. As to what was being said by Mr. Babic in respect to what I said about lists, again, there seems to have been, perhaps, by Mr. Babic some misunderstanding of how these lists operated. The position so far, and this is on recollection - I haven't been able to check the point because I didn't know it was going to be raised - but so far as my recollection is concerned, there was one -- let me go back. Mr. Babic says they were not all dead. The larger list of 100 names was derived from a list provided by the Serbian authorities of 200 plus people or bodies that they recorded as having been deposited in mass graves over a limited number of days. Of that, and I think it was 200 plus, 100 could be identified by name. These were the names that were put to every witness in extensive form by the Defence, and I think one name did show up as a person who was still alive. I remember he was a butcher in another town. And whether there was confusion over the name or whether it was somebody having the same name, but so there was one name and, in my recollection, one name only of all those lists prepared in the different ways who may have been shown still to be alive. I would have checked this more fully if I'd had advance notice. I now turn to the matters that have been argued this morning. First, on this aspect of the case there can be no doubt that there was full argument by both sides to the Trial Chamber on the issue of sentence with the calling of evidence, extensive evidence, by the Defence. Obviously, this Chamber is in a position, if it wishes to, to read the arguments advanced from both sides and, cogently as I recall them, by Mr. Greaves then appearing for the appellant Jelisic. I see that there is no complaint on the basis now of material provided to the Trial Chamber, but can I -- there's one remaining complaint, but there's no complaint about the material provided. I'll come back to the matter of complaint in a minute. The materials provided to the Chamber by the Prosecution included an extensive skeleton that they could follow, a text they could follow of the submissions we were making. That text did not become part of the record. It was for reference purposes and then, no doubt, to be in due course discarded. To that text there was an analysis of -- attached to that text there was analysis of some of the Defence witnesses, and there was another extensive tabular analysis of the evidence that related to the pleas of guilty side by side to what the appellant had said in the interviews with investigators in relation to those matters. And the material was made available to the Trial Chamber in this way because this had the potential for being confusing material, and it needed to be available in a side-by-side basis so that the Chamber could look at each individual killing and say, "This was the evidence in relation to that killing, and this is what the appellant said about it." Now, one complaint or perhaps two were made. First, there's the suggestion that there was an agreed basis of facts between the parties in respect of the pleas of guilty. It is true there was a document so titled, a very slim document which simply reflected the pleas that were going to be tendered and said in a sentence or so the defendant took two brothers or one brother outside and shot him. Simply not enough factual material for any Trial Chamber to pass sentence because it was a bare assertion of an activity. When that document was served in 1998, and it was amended but in the most insignificant way for these purposes I think in October of 1998, it was recognised by those then conducting the case, Mr. Bowers and Mr. Tochilovsky, that the Chamber would require further assistance if and when or when it came to deal with the pleas. And so a further appendix was served at that time as a filing, and that contained extracts from material witnesses whose evidence would have touched on individual crimes to which the appellant had made admissions, and it also contained some fuller witness statements covering the same topic as a confidential annex. So that the Chamber had for its consideration of sentence, it had this raw material that was always known to be the basis upon which the Prosecution would present material as under Rule 100 to assist the Chamber. It had full argument, and it had, of course, the evidence in the genocide trial. It then had the tools of analysis to which I have referred. I can tell Your Honours that, and I hope that the Court will accept it because the tools provided were not part of the record, but the very large majority of material relating to the pleas of guilty was evidence that had been given in the genocide trial, and the other way around, in the genocide trial, evidence reflecting the matters to which he had pleaded guilty was very much the majority of the evidence. There was other evidence, but comparatively little, so that there was no risk of, or no significant risk of infection of the Chamber by that additional material it had heard in the genocide trial. First of all, one can trust that the Chamber knew what its duty was. But in any event, all the materials focused on these matters to which the appellant had pleaded guilty, and the tools with which they were provided, I trust, would have assisted them in that exercise. I have to say that the exercise I then had to perform before the Trial Chamber, that is, not an exercise in mitigation of sentence with which common law lawyers are much more familiar but an exercise in identifying the gravity of the offence, is not one which necessarily comes very naturally to common law advocates. It's still a strange experience. It's our argument that neither those of us presenting the case nor the investigators who had to give some assistance to the Chamber on issues of gravity had any desire or any purpose to serve in making the picture worse than it was. The sole purpose at all times was to try and get the correct picture of the gravity of the crimes and of the nature of the appellant. If I could turn to the twin issues of the interviews, which I can deal with in open court and the other aspect of the matter which I may have to deal with briefly in a closed session, on those twin issues, the Chamber may be assisted by the material evidence of the investigator O'Donnell, given on day 19 and, in my pagination if it's correct, starting at 2066, where at two passages - one, 2083 and one, 2169 - he dealt with these issues for the assistance of the Trial Chamber in the course of dealing with the interviews. I shan't go over his answers extensively, and I would invite the Chamber if it finds this a helpful issue to read them, because they are not very long. He was given, the Chamber may conclude, a balanced view, explaining, first, so far as the interviews are concerned, that yes, he was -- that the appellant was giving, it appeared, a sanitised version. They were taking time with the appellant because they were concerned, of course, to contrast what the appellant was saying with the independent material they had, witness statements and the like, that was at odds with what he was saying. Indeed, one of the problems of the interviews was, lengthy though they were, that the appellant was setting the agenda himself and declining altogether to be interviewed on certain topics. For example, he declined altogether to be interviewed about genocide as a particular topic, but there were other controls he made. Indeed, it appears that it was when they were going, in the last interview, to deal with further inconsistencies that it was the appellant who stopped the interview process. Nevertheless, within that process, the officers identified inconsistencies both within the interviews themselves, going to show doubt on the man's true candor, and real inconsistencies between what he was saying in mitigating his role and what was available from independent sources. So there is every reason for the Chamber to have taken the very cautious view that it may have taken in respect of credit to be given for this aspect of cooperation and plea. Can I turn, briefly, perhaps in closed session for safety, to the other aspect which has been raised particularly by Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I move on to a couple of points about plea of guilty. The Chamber was entirely justified, in our respectful submission, in placing very little reliance on that in light of what it observed, first, about the photograph sequence. I referred to this yesterday. It's the photograph sequence of the appellant executing someone, several photographs of him and of how he does it. He couldn't deny that. As the Chamber will readily understand, by the presentation to him in interview of witness statements that identify him with absolute clarity, it was beyond doubt he may have judged that he had no defence to nearly all the matters that are the subject matter of his pleas of guilty. There is no automatic entitlement, and it can be outweighed by aggravating circumstances. Of course, Kambanda pleaded guilty and, as we know, received the maximum sentence of life imprisonment. A few other points. As to whether he was, was regarded as, or should ever have been advanced as a commander, it was never suggested that he was the actual commander of the Luka camp, the third place where he was seen - first, the police station; second, briefly, the Laser bus station; and then the killings at Luka - never suggested he was the commander there. The contrary. The Prosecution's case was, in the trial, that of course he was acting pursuant to a plan and, as a matter of inevitable inference, as a subordinate to others who were the architects, as it is said, of the plan and who were commanding him. Indeed, we relied upon the facts that he referred to himself in interview of his recruitment and of his supervision. So there was never any suggestion that he was the actual commander of the Luka camp. Yes, one or two witnesses assumed he was, and there may have even been words said to suggest that he was. But the clear body of evidence both from him and from the victim witnesses was to the effect that he was working together with others - the inspectors who carried out brief interrogations in particular will come to mind - and that showed that they were all working within a regime of which it was not suggested he was the chief. Of course, he had extensive de facto power within that regime, and it may be he had command, certainly when he had the gun in his hand, over some of the others who assisted him. But that is not to say that we suggested, and we did not, that he was the commander of the camp. That matters not at all and, in our respectful submission, was, must have been, and plainly was fully understood by the Trial Chamber. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. A couple of things about personality and remorse. The suggestion, incidentally, that he didn't and couldn't have given evidence is probably not accurate. Given the extensive nature of sentencing proceedings, there is nothing to stop an accused giving evidence at that stage on his own behalf in explanation of what he had admitted. Nothing to stop that. The evidence in respect of remorse or the material properly available in respect of remorse was probably not limited strictly to evidence from the witness chair, for in a long trial, a Chamber has an opportunity to consider a man even if he remains silent. I don't exclude the possibility that the Trial Chamber will have made some assessments of him, both his presence and the occasions when he chose to absent himself. As to the spoken or written evidence, apart from what individual witnesses said, and to those I will turn for the sentence or so per witness in a second, as to the other spoken or written evidence, it was nearly all one way. The psychiatric evidence, apart from the very brief reference slightly misquoted in the footnote of the judgement as to a page reference but matters not about that, of the Dr. Van den Bussche, the evidence was all one way: No remorse. Van den Bussche, and it suggests that it's page 22, but the relevant document only runs to page 17, and it's on that page that the doctor, who had a short second examination of the appellant, said, "He would appear more than in the past to demonstrate remorse." The same report of the doctor, which is part of the record for you to consider, made it plain in various ways that his concerns were almost exclusively for himself. He gave various examples of what the appellant said to him about crying and matters of that sort while in custody, but it all emerged that these were focused on himself, thus really giving support not to the very low level of conclusion "would appear more than in the past to have remorse" but would have supported the other findings about the personality defects, limited though they may have been, of this appellant at the time he examined him. Accordingly, there was no reason for the Chamber to take other than the view they clearly did, in our respectful submission, about remorse and to discount it in the way that they properly did. Again, without wishing to trouble you with researching passages of transcript, there was a day, I think it was the last day of evidence, when both doctors were examined and cross-examined, and if there's any concern about the issue that's raised on remorse related to the psychiatric evidence, I would invite the Chamber to at least consider reviewing that material, which of course I'm not going to review any more than to the degree I have already. Remorse, I have to say, was also countered by a piece of evidence to which I must turn, if I may, in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Without dwelling on it, one of the other features of the evidence overall that may have lain behind the Trial Chamber's rejection of what was being urged as mitigation, was that despite these extensive interviews and despite every opportunity to call witnesses made available to the Defence, the picture of what this man did, both before arriving at Brcko, the year or so before when we know he was convicted of some comparatively small crime, and what he did afterwards before arrest was wholly unarticulated and unclear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The screens, the screens suggest that we are still in closed session. Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The picture both before and after was wholly unclear. The picture of his recruitment before when in a very short space of time he either rose so as to become somebody who committed these crimes or threw himself willingly as being one of these people who could commit crimes, the picture after when he could have shown genuine remorse and he could have surrendered himself, were both entirely unclear, consistent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- with the position taken by the Prosecution and, it appears, adopted by the Chamber that he was not candid. He was not honest, particularly in relation to the things he dealt with in his interviews, where, for example, he said he didn't look at people when he was killing them and he said, "If anybody had asked me not to kill them, I wouldn't have killed them;" countered by stretches of evidence of people pleading for their lives at the moment that he executed them himself. And you can see all this in the schedule I provided yesterday. There was material to find that he was not candid and was dishonest. And the extent of material available to the Chamber, carefully argued on the day of closing submissions, and as we see from their judgement in summary form, plainly reviewed by them on this topic, it's our submission that they performed their sentencing assessment correctly with all the material there to help them, and the decisions they reached factually are beyond reproach. And that in light of the jurisprudence that my learned friend Mr. Guariglia has reminded you of and has -- and as has been advanced in our written brief, the sentence imposed was not a day too long and should be sustained. That's all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: One question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Actually, I have two questions for Mr. Guariglia and one for Mr. Nice, but since Mr. Nice is on his feet, why don't I take that one the first. If I understand one of the appellant's arguments, and I would like your reaction to it, it is that though he pleaded on the basis of an agreed statement of facts to a second indictment setting out the crimes against humanity, some of the evidence which came in during the genocide aspect of the case which dealt with some of the particularly gruesome aspects of some of the crimes which was not repeated in the statement of facts to which he pled guilty on those crimes, were in fact taken into consideration in the sentencing. I just want your comments on that argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Can I go back to what I said earlier, and it's my error for not perhaps making it adequately plain. The agreed statement of facts dated the 9th of September -- signed and dated the 9th of September of 1998 was terse in the extreme. I take an example. Counts 6 and 7, "Goran Jelisic will plead guilty to Counts 6 and 7 and admit that, on or about the 6th or 7th of May, 1992, he escorted an unknown male detainee down a street near the Brcko police station and then shot him in the head with a Scorpion pistol." Now, that is the way individual offences were summarised. That apart, there was no narrative giving an agreed version of background or even foreground to these offences. And as I suggested at an earlier stage this morning, the material here was far too limited, and, for assessment, for purposes of guilt, it was the bare bones of what he was pleading to. It wasn't an overall agreed version of facts on the basis of which the Prosecution could present the case to the Trial Chamber, bearing in mind its various duties. That led to the presentation of the annex to which I have earlier referred which was presented to the Chamber by a filing on the 29th of September, and I'll just read it because I don't think it's going to be before you. It says this: "In accordance with Judge Riad's request during the Status Conference of the 2nd of September of the parties to reach agreement on admitted and disputed facts, Jelisic has expressed an intention to plead guilty." Paragraph 2: "The Prosecution and Defence jointly submitted the agreed factual basis for the guilty pleas." Paragraph 3, and this is the only other paragraph: "In order to assist the Trial Chamber in evaluating the factual basis for the guilty pleas, the Prosecution submits excerpts from Prosecution witness statements and interviews held with Jelisic on specific counts of the amended indictment to which he intends to plead guilty as Annex 1, and a supplementary report, complete witness statements, and relevant pages of interviews held with Goran Jelisic are attached in confidential Annex 2"; so that immediately after the agreed but exiguous statement of facts, we have this larger document. Now, it was never signed by the Defence, that's true, but it was always claimed that it was the intention of the Prosecution to present such material to the Chamber as may have been required to flesh out those one or two lines that were in the agreed statement of facts. And can I then take you to page 27 of our respondent's brief -- I'm sorry, that's right. I'm looking at it in Mr. Guariglia's version so I'm not familiar with where it appears in the binder. What happened on the 19th of October, without complaint - we can find it at paragraph 4.6, page 27 - is that I told the Chamber that there is this large document, a bundle of witness statements served at the time of the guilty plea and to support the plea, it is either witness statements or extracts from witness statements both, and we will rely on without calling those witnesses as part of the material for the sentencing purpose. That was not complained of. In short, the parties all knew and agreed that the plea would be Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. dealt with without calling live evidence circumscribed to the particular counts in the indictment and that we would rely on this written material. So as to infection by material wider than the agreed statement of facts, in response to Your Honour's particular question, first by agreement and understanding, there was this body of written material to which the Court could refer. That doesn't, of course, deal with the other half of Your Honour's question: What about the trial? As I say, in relation to that, one can trust the Chamber to have excised it from consideration because they realised they had to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you. I do have one question for Mr. Guariglia too. You emphasised the Trial Chamber's discretion in sentencing because so many of these cases have very individualised characteristics, and you yourself contrasted Erdemovic from Mr. Jelisic. I'm wondering, however, given the great emphasis that Mr. Clegg placed on Tadic, which, it seems to me, is somewhat more similar than Mr. Erdemovic, and conceding your argument that that alone -- that a Trial Chamber doesn't have to look at what happened in every other case, nonetheless, I would find it helpful if you would give me your argument or impressions of why the sentence, which was changed by the Appellate Chamber in Tadic, would merit only half the time given here. Along with that would be the more abstract question: Is your argument that two Trial Chambers in this Tribunal, given, for hypothesis' sake, the same circumstances of crimes, the same youth, all the other factors, that nonetheless they would be justified in giving quite different sentences just based upon the way the evidence struck them?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUARIGLIA
utterances.text: Your Honour, as far as the first question is concerned, it is dangerous to engage in an exercise of comparison of cases without having at your disposal all of the elements of all the cases, and to be in a position to determine, off the cuff, whether the culpability of the perpetrators was the same. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You [Realtime transcript read in error "I"] did it with Erdemovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUARIGLIA
utterances.text: I did it with Erdemovic, as you said, and with Tadic, I will do it off the cuff, to some extent. We would submit that if, in Erdemovic, there seemed to be a subjective difference, a difference in the subjective field, it is clear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: May I ask that the transcript should be corrected. We have, as against Judge Wald, this statement: "I did it with Erdemovic." I believe she said, "You did it with Erdemovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUARIGLIA
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour. Going back to what I was about to say, between Erdemovic and Jelisic, the argument can be made, and this is the Prosecution's position, that there is a subjective difference. The perpetrators are different. Between Tadic and Jelisic, we would submit there is a very significant objective difference in the scope of victimisation in both cases. In the case of Tadic, you have two killings and then Tadic's participation in a number of events of beatings. In the case of the appellant in these proceedings, you have the appellant actively engaged in a significant number of killings, committed in the most brutal manner and in the context a confined system of ill-treatment at the Luka camp, and previously the police station. We think that the level of victimisation is different between the two cases and that the Trial Chamber had the authority to attach to that particular degree and intensity of victimisation a different sentence than the one imposed in the Tadic case. I don't know if that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUARIGLIA
utterances.text: As far as your second question is concerned, there is no doubt -- let me put it this way: No doubt it would be desirable that sentences from Trial Chambers in the International Tribunal in very similar cases don't present fundamental disparities. However, some degree of disparity is a natural consequence of the exercise of discretion by the Trial Chambers and of the fact that the parameters offered by the Statute and the Rules are broad parameters. But at the same time that this appellate Court has said, for the purposes of establishing errors of fact, that two reasonable Judges may look at the same evidence with different eyes, and provided they move both within the same scope of reasonable judicial activity, deference must be given to the trier of fact. We submit a similar conclusion may be reached in the case of sentencing. Providing that Trial Chamber A has moved within the parameters of the Statute and the Rules and has reasonably exercised its discretion, yes, it may be that the sentence in a very similar case by Trial Chamber B will be different; but provided both Trial Chambers act reasonably, within the boundaries of their authority as granted by the Statute and the Rules, those two sentences should remain undisturbed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUARIGLIA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Guariglia, just to clear my mind on it and because Erdemovic has been so frequently referred to, may I ask whether your impression is the same as my recollection, my rather rusty recollection, of the Erdemovic case. Am I right in feeling that there are two things about that case: One, Erdemovic gave himself up to the Tribunal at the time when the Tribunal was not even aware of his existence or of the possibility of any allegations being made against him; two, the Prosecution in fact, I believe, conceded that he had acted under duress. The matter went to the Court of Appeal on this basis, that for Erdemovic, it was argued that duress was a complete defence. The Court of Appeal said, No, no, it is not a complete defence. What can happen, however, is that duress may be taken in mitigation. So the case assumed that posture when it went back, and Erdemovic was given a five-year sentence. Are those factors present in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUARIGLIA
utterances.text: They are not, Your Honour, and that is the position, that subjectively the cases are completely different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Clegg, you will finish by 1.00?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I would hope to finish very soon after 1.00. But could I ask for the indulgence of the Chamber for five minutes. Mr. Jelisic has indicated he just wants to have a brief word with me. It's difficult as I don't speak the same language, and if I could have five minutes, I would still hope to finish comfortably before 1.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We would like to accommodate Mr. Clegg. May I have a moment to consult with colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: My colleague, Judge Nieto, thinks that, in principle, we ought to have the recess. I was under the assumption that you will go on for some time after 1.00. About how long, even with the five minutes' recess, how long would you be after 1.00?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I would hope to conclude in under 15 minutes, and then Mr. Babic will deal with the points that touch on the particular aspect of the appeal which he has covered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We better recess then --

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: -- and we better recess now; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So you can have your five minutes during the recess period.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: That will certainly avoid any pressure of time that I have with Mr. Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. The court stands suspended. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.45 p.m. 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The proceedings are resumed. I would like to extend my deepest apologies for the delay. Mr. Clegg.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: It's our submission that the Prosecution approach is, frankly, unhelpful to this Tribunal. They argue that, and I quote, "The alleged need to recognise a tariff for a sentence does not exist." As a bold statement of fact, that is, we submit, completely unsustainable. We venture to suggest that the reason why the Prosecution advances their argument on that basis is because they recognise that no application of any tariff can survive examination with the sentence passed in this case. In order to illustrate what we submit is post-sentence diplomacy, one is only to look at the argument that they advanced in the Celebici Judgement that was to the exact reverse of that which was advanced today. At paragraph 715 in the Celebici Judgement, the Prosecution made the opposite submission, exactly the same as the one I advanced today and directly contrary to the one they have advanced. What they said was, the Prosecution submits that the Appeal Chamber should determine, "Basic sentencing principles which will be applied by the Trial Chamber. The Appeal Chamber notes the Prosecution made similar submissions"; then gives detail of a further case before the Appeals Chamber, arguing, and I quote, "That such principles would assist in order to achieve consistency and even handedness in sentencing before the Trial Chamber." Those words, with respect, don't lie easily with the answer given to Her Honour Judge Wald before lunch. Those arguments advanced by the Prosecution in the Celebici case were, of course, advanced in an appeal against sentence that could be sustained by an application of comparison with the tariff as it has developed. And I do venture to suggest that the adoption of a diametrically opposite stance today reflects the recognition that this sentence is so out of step with the jurisprudence of this Court and the Tribunal for Rwanda that they are, by adopting the stance they do, acknowledging the paucity of their submission. The Tadic Judgement at page 55 -- sorry, paragraph 55 on page 24 allowed the appeal - it was the only ground, as my memory serves me, upon which the sentence was reduced on the merits as opposed to arguments about when time should run -- allowed the appeal and reduced from 25 to 20 the sentence for this reason: because it failed to adequately consider the need for sentences to reflect the relative significance of the role of the appellant in the broader context of the conflict in the former Yugoslavia. The ground of appeal that I was advancing before the Appeal Chamber in that case read as follows, that the Trial Chamber had fell into error with respect to the need to develop a range of sentences based upon the relative position of the accused and, I might add in addition to that, the role that he played. So we do, with respect, invite the Court to consider the response of the Prosecution to our submissions on tariff as, at the very least, being economical. Curiously, when it came to the Erdemovic Judgement, the Prosecution were only too happy to point out the tariff principle did not apply. There is merit in their argument on that ground, and I acknowledge that. The facts were entirely different. Had it not been for Judge Wald, not one word would have been said by them about the Tadic Judgement, upon which I relied heavily in my oral submissions. What was said to Judge Wald was wrong. It is quite untrue to say that Tadic was only convicted of two murders. The Appellant Chamber reversed two acquittals for murder of the two policemen in the village in question, the name which escapes me, whose throats Tadic had slit. But that was, of course, in addition to the other murders that he had been convicted of, including the five in the village of Jelisca. I apologise for the almost inevitable mispronunciation of that name. I would invite the Court to consider the original sentencing judgement in Tadic to obtain a fair view of the crimes that Tadic had been convicted of; to look at the conclusions of the appeal against conviction which convicted him of a number of offences of which he had hitherto been found not guilty; and then look at the appeal against sentence in order to see whether or not there is any merit at all in the submission made that a real or sensible distinction can be drawn between the two cases. We confidently submit that if the Court were to take the trouble, as I know it will, to look at those documents, then the Court will be inevitably driven to the conclusion that no sensible distinction can be drawn. It seemed inconsistent, with the way Judge Wald's question was answered, to reflect upon what the Prosecution were themselves saying in the Tadic Sentencing Appeal. What they were then taking to the Appeals Chamber was, and I quote, "The respondent contends that in assessing the circumstances relevant to the appellant, the Trial Chamber also considered the brutality of the acts in which he personally engaged and his willingness to take part in the ethnic cleansing which occurred in the area," an argument advanced with all of the adjectives properly appended to the conduct of this appellant today. Rank, it was suggested in oral argument, was of no importance. Indeed, it was suggested that the fact that Jelisic was of low rank or, more accurately, no rank was not a matter to be taken into account. That is entirely inconsistent with the view of this Appeals Chamber in the Tadic Judgement. Of course they are right when they say that a person must be punished for the crimes he has committed not the rank he held. That isn't the reason why rank is distinguished in sentence. Had Hitler been alive at the end of the war, the Court may be confident that he would have received a heavier sentence than a member of a single Einzatgruppen commando unit that was responsible for ethnic cleansing in eastern Europe. Why? Hitler never killed anybody with his own hands, so far as we know, but he would have received the ultimate penalty because it was his position in the command structure of the Third Reich that set in motion the acts that were put into place by others. It is that position of command, not the fact that he never touched the hair of any one Jew's head, that would have meant he should have paid and would have paid the ultimate penalty. The reason why rank commands a higher penalty is not because the person of high rank is punished more for doing the same act, it is because the fact that they are in a position of high rank which enables them to influence affairs over a much wider ambit than somebody of low or no rank. It is the use of that influence that is essential for any ethnic cleansing programme to operate, and it is the use of it by men of rank that commands higher sentences than mere foot soldiers. It is, we respectfully submit, a distinction that the Prosecution refuse to recognise for the same reason as they refuse to recognise the need for a tariff because they know this sentence cannot survive examination. Just a word or two about the evidence before Mr. Babic deals with the matters that he is going to. The agreed factual basis is, of course, going to be fleshed out by the evidence relating to the individual counts upon which he has pleaded. I accept entirely what Mr. Nice says so far as that is concerned. But insofar as the evidence embraces allegations that have not been the subject of any admission of guilt and did not result in any conviction, then they must be put out of the mind of the Trial Chamber when it turns to sentence. Insofar as the evidence did, as it did at trial, embrace a far wider criminal allegation, namely, of genocide, then we submit that that ought to be ignored save and insofar as it is directly relevant to the individual counts to which the accused has pleaded. Finally, we do not accept the summary of evidence as presented by Mr. Nice as either fair or accurate. It is redolent of problems for me to select individual passages from the transcripts that point in the opposite direction. We would just invite the Court to consider the evidence of six Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. witnesses not particularly long before coming to a decision as to the effect of the witnesses to whom he spoke; they are DA, DE, DH, DK, DO, and DQ. If the Court would glance at those transcripts, we would respectfully submit that the interpretation put on them by Mr. Nice cannot fairly be sustained. That is all I seek to say by way of reply, subject to the words of Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Clegg. Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall try to respect the time limit set by Your Honours and be as concise as possible. We did not draw attention to an incorrectness in the sentence and that is the killing of the Zahirevic brothers. In paragraphs 37 and 38 of the judgement, Goran is alleged to have killed both Zahirevic brothers, and this is also contained in the disposition; the second amended indictment alleges that Goran Jelisic killed only one Zahirevic brother, and this is also contained in the agreed statement of facts signed by both parties. So I appeal to the Appeals Chamber to bear this fact in mind and also to take into consideration when determining the sentence. Secondly, we accept with satisfaction the position of the Prosecution that the document to which the Defence -- the document referred to was not signed by the Defence, though earlier on it was claimed that it was a joint document. This is also stated in paragraph 18, footnote 9. So I ask Your Honours also to take that into consideration. Of special interest to me is why the Prosecution has not referred to the Defence witnesses. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: (redacted). If the primary aim of the judgements of this Tribunal is to achieve reconciliation, then it was the duty of the Defence and of the Prosecution to bear that in mind to show that people can still live together, that they can do some good things to each other, and that that can serve as a basis for their joint life in the future. The statement by the Prosecution that they never said that Jelisic was the camp commander is something that can easily be disproved. Both the first and the second amended indictment contained Counts 50 and 51, and those counts say: "Goran Jelisic, acting as camp commander of the Luka camp, created an atmosphere of fear, killing, mistreating, and threatening detainees, whereby he subjected them to extreme psychological trauma, degradation, and fear of physical injury and death." These counts and descriptions and allegations were later reversed by the Prosecution, and the amended indictment does not contain them, and we are glad to accept that the Prosecution agrees in the fact that Jelisic was not a camp commander. The Prosecution claims today there was nothing more than a plea of guilt, but let me add that regarding the agreed statement of facts between the Prosecution, which was represented by other Prosecutors and the Defence, a number of meetings were held, and only once all those facts had been thrashed out and when the Prosecution accepted the plea of Goran Jelisic as agreed, only then was that agreement signed. Therefore, the second document that the Prosecution is relying on cannot disclaim this first joint document. So one could put it this way: For the moment, we'll agree, but we'll act as if we are working on the basis of the previous document, which is quite different. And I must say, with all due respect, that that is not fair, and it is also not in accordance with the instructions given by His Honour Judge Jorda to the parties at the Status Conference held on the 23rd of September, 1998, when this agreement was being negotiated. So I would appeal to Your Honours to refer to the transcript of that Status Conference. And the last point that I would like to make I would like to do in private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We're now in public session. I take it that closes the arguments --

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: -- for Mr. Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Then before the Appeals Chamber withdraws to consider its decision, there are perhaps one or two points I might mention. One has to do with the skeleton arguments submitted by the Defence. We have referred to that, but since we will be in need of it possibly for the preparation of a judgement, would you help to clarify the position as to whether that document has been formally laid over or not? Is it part of the record?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: It is part of the record, I assume, because it has been circulated to all parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Fine, then that is part of the record. The other thing I want to refer to concerns your reference to the Celebici Judgement and to that part of it which dealt with cumulative convictions. I think the Prosecution said that they might want to file a statement, but my understanding of the position was that they would wish to file a statement only if you pursued the point, and I don't recall that the point was pursued. Was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: It was pursued in the sense that having raised the matter, my reading of the judgement would indicate that it was applicable to the convictions in this case, and therefore we would pursue it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Good. Then we'll ask the Prosecution what time they would judge to be convenient for the filing of their statement on the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. As my learned friend mentions that it was taken up as a matter of appeal now, to respond to the applicability of the judgement to the issues in this case, we would say we would require about ten days' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Ten days?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Clegg, thereafter what period would suit you for a reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: Ten days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Ten plus ten, that's twenty. Okay, then, that is settled. All right. Then I come to the last thing on my shopping list which has been presented to me by the secretary, and it has to do, Mr. Clegg, with your offer to comply with the Scheduling Order of the 30th of January calling upon both sides to file public versions of certain documents. There are two documents in respect to which public versions have not yet been filed by the Defence. One is the appellant's brief in the appellant's -- the cross appellant's appeal dated 7 August 2000, and the other one is his reply dated 6 October 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. CLEGG
utterances.text: I have very helpfully been provided with an unmarked copy of each of those by the registry yesterday. We will file a redacted copy within ten days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Ten days. All right, let it be so written. That, then, concludes the hearing, and the Bench wishes to express thanks to both sides for very able and helpful arguments. We will reserve decision, and you will be both notified in due course.
